rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast scouting gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

The first method already achieves the maximum CRF, with substantial resolution margin. Shorten the gradient while holding composition endpoints and temperature fixed to seek a faster fully resolved separation.
Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test a faster separation while preserving the maximum CRF. The current minimum resolution of 2.54 leaves some margin above the 1.5 target.

Test the shortest allowed gradient to establish the speed limit at these endpoints and temperature. The first pair may fall below 1.5; if so, the fully resolved 4-minute gradient remains the fallback.

Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing the maximum CRF. This also measures the temperature sensitivity of the critical early pair.

Cooling should improve the early pair’s selectivity, while lowering the endpoint makes the 2-minute gradient less steep. Test whether this combination restores full resolution with a last peak earlier than the current fully resolved 4.14-minute result.

Raise the final organic fraction one grid step to accelerate the last peak while testing the early pair’s narrow resolution margin. Injection 6 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback if the steeper gradient drops that pair below 1.5.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce the gradient slope while retaining the stronger endpoint. Test whether this recovers the early pair’s small resolution deficit and keeps the last peak earlier than in injection 6.

Shift both endpoints upward while preserving the slope that gave full resolution in injection 8. The stronger endpoint should accelerate the last peak; this tests whether the early pair remains resolved at the higher starting organic fraction.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention further while keeping the maximum endpoint and minimum gradient duration. Monitor the early pair for loss of retention or resolution as it approaches the dead-time region.

Raise temperature one step to accelerate the last peak while testing whether the early pair’s resolution margin remains sufficient. Injection 10 provides a fully resolved fallback if warming lowers the minimum resolution below 1.5.

Raise the starting organic fraction one grid step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation. This tests whether the shallower gradient preserves early-pair resolution or whether reduced initial retention becomes limiting.

Return to the starting composition that preserved early retention and test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method. This brackets the temperature limit for maintaining CRF 1.000 at the minimum gradient duration.

Lower the endpoint one step to test whether a shallower gradient restores early-pair resolution at 35 C. Compare the resulting last-peak time with injection 11, which remains the fastest method achieving the maximum CRF.

Lower both endpoints relative to injection 11, preserving its gradient slope while moving the early pair away from the pre-gradient elution region. Test for a fully resolved alternative with greater initial retention and only a modest late-peak time cost.

Test whether cooling restores early-pair resolution at the higher starting organic fraction that failed at 30 C. This checks the remaining nearby composition boundary while retaining injection 11 as the fastest fully resolved method.

Refine around injection 11 by lowering the endpoint one step, seeking additional resolution margin with a small retention-time cost. The maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a nearby fully resolved alternative without repeating a method.

Test a shallower gradient with a higher starting organic fraction as a potentially more robust maximum-CRF alternative. Injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved method; this run seeks greater critical-pair resolution while keeping all peaks comfortably within 10 minutes.

Lower the starting organic fraction one step from injection 18 to improve early-pair retention and test for greater resolution margin. This refines a short, maximum-CRF alternative while retaining injection 11 as the fastest fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one grid step from injection 19 to shorten retention while testing its remaining early-pair resolution margin. Keep injection 11 as the fastest maximum-CRF method if this warmer alternative falls below full resolution.

Return to the fast 2-minute-gradient region and cool injection 17 by one step to seek a larger early-pair resolution margin. This should provide another maximum-CRF option near the fastest fully resolved method without repeating an injection.

Cool injection 15 by one grid step to increase early-pair selectivity while retaining a fast separation and better initial retention than at phi0 0.30. The maximum score is already achieved; injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved method.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 15 to test a faster separation at the lower starting organic fraction. This fills the nearest untested condition around injection 11, the fastest method attaining CRF 1.000.

Shift both endpoints down one step from injection 9 to test a fast, fully resolved alternative with more initial retention. Injection 11 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method; this run checks the nearby lower-organic operating margin.

Use the final injection to test a shallower gradient near proven maximum-CRF conditions, seeking more early-pair resolution margin while retaining a short separation. Injection 11 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, with CRF 1.000 and the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
